chapter_theme: Natrinai 141-160: the night path and its dangers, feared by the woman (144, 154, 158) and refused or redirected by the friend (151, 156); the house that learns, through a mother's scent of hair (143), a girl's guilty denial (147), the town's gossip and the cane (145, 149); the madal rider's public ride (146, 152); men held back or summoned home by a woman's hair and season (141, 142, 157); separation borne (148, 153); first wonder and its answer (155, 160); a courtesan's mockery (150); and the friend's demands for marriage (159).

141.reading: The man tells his heart, bent on going for wealth, that the hard dry tract where long-podded konrai trees, rubbed by rain-season elephants muddy from wallowing, stand together in the heat like unbathed hill ascetics with long matted locks, would be easy for it; but he will not leave her spreading, thick hair, like the cool dark ripples of the Arisil that runs round Ambar of the tall flags, town of Killi, famous for his tusked elephants that fought chariots while kites wheeled above.
141.nuance: மன் in line 7 makes the ease counterfactual: the road would be easy, if he could go. The ascetic simile turns the konrai, a rain-season tree of the mullai, into figures of renunciation standing in the waste, which is exactly what he declines to become.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சிற்குத் தலைவன் சொல்லிச் செலவு அழுங்கியது

thinai_evidence.note: a man weighing a journey through the waste for wealth, and refusing it

comparisons.tenor: the konrai trees, their long dry pods like matted hair, standing together unwashed in the heat
her spreading dark hair

142.reading: Returning with his task done, the man tells his charioteer that her town lies in the woodland of unfailing plenty, where at the end of the rains a milk-trading herdsman, his rope-sling, fire-drill and pot bundled with a hide on his back, stands on one leg propped on his staff in the drizzle, whistling through folded lips to settle his small-headed flock; there lives the gentle young woman whose chastity befits the mullai, who rejoices when a guest comes even at night.
142.nuance: The herdsman holding still in the rain to keep his flock together is the picture of patient keeping that the last three lines give to the wife; and the praise he chooses is her welcome to guests at night, a householder's virtue, not her beauty.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsman, his flock and the woodland, with the wife's waiting chastity

comparisons.tenor: her chastity, which waits as the mullai land waits for the rains

143.reading: The mother, faint, says that every time she sees the swept sand of the fine courtyard, the girl's playmates and the nochchi, her eyes run with tears; yet the girl who called even her parrot kin is without fault: in the few days when she heard the cruel sweet talk of the gossiping women gathered in the old town, she lived on as if she did not know, and said only, 'your hair smells fragrant'.
143.nuance: The last line is a confession: the scent of her daughter's hair was the sign of a lover, and the mother, already hearing the gossip, let it pass with a remark. She clears the girl (வழு இலள்) and keeps the fault for herself.

thinai_evidence.note: the mother weeps in the house the girl has left

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; by the poem the mother, speaking to no one present and at the end to the absent girl

144.reading: With the man listening nearby, the woman tells her friend that as the dark she-elephant, when a tiger attacks her great bull, shrinks from the uproar as from the roar of massed rain-clouds, so her own flower-like eyes stream and her foolish heart frets, now that she knows he comes by night, flowers pressed on his shoulders, alone across the hard forked paths where the gaping tigress prowls and the deep pools of the fast forest stream are hard to cross.
144.nuance: Lines 1 to 2 can also be read as the beginning of the scene she fears rather than a matched picture; either way the she-elephant's fear for her mate stands next to the woman's fear for hers.

thinai_evidence.note: elephant, tiger and hill stream of the night path

comparisons.tenor: the uproar of the tiger's attack, heard as thunder
her kohl eyes

iraicchi.act: the she-elephant, when the tiger attacks her bull, is terrified for him
iraicchi.sense: the woman's fear for the man crossing tiger country by night is the fear even a beast feels for its mate, so it is love, not weakness, and he should end it

145.reading: With the man listening, the friend tells the woman that their unjust mother, even before their bond with the handsome shore lord, where on the wet white sand by the dark backwater women add the large purple blossoms of the adumbu creeper to their garlands, had grown at all close, spoke as if she had already lain with him and asked where she had been; she has a right to read the change in their looks, and now even in the dead of night the bells of his chariot come softly to their punnai-lined street.
145.nuance: The midnight chariot bells are told to the man who drives the chariot: the house now hears what the mother only suspected, and the only way out of the suspicion is marriage.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்து தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாக தோழி வரைவுகடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: backwater, adumbu creeper and punnai of the shore

146.reading: Speaking so the friend will hear, the man who keeps following addresses a rider of the tall palmyra-stem horse, crowned with flowers no one would sell and roaming town after town as one well smitten: if he will take his word, let him come down a little into a tree's shade as cool as the umbrella of a king who knows his duty and rest before he goes on while the sun moves, for kind people will gather round him; such is the deluded heart that the dark girl, lovely as if painted by a master, has struck.
146.nuance: வில்லாப் பூ, the flower no one sells, is the erukku of the madal garland, named by what it is not. The colophon calls the poem kurinji; by its matter, the madal, it is the perunthinai of the Tholkappiyam.

thinai_evidence.note: the palmyra-stem horse and its flowers, the lover's public ride of the madal

comparisons.tenor: the cool tree shade offered to the madal rider
the dark girl's beauty, as if painted
the palmyra stem he rides

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is a madal rider, the speaker's own case shown as another's (முன்னிலைப் புறமொழி)

147.reading: With the man listening, the friend tells the girl of the bright forehead that they are done for: when their mother scolded her, asking where she had gone while the red-beaked green parrots carried off the heavy millet heads on the honeyed slope, she stood before her and said she neither knew nor had ever seen the lord of the great waterfall hills, nor plucked flowers with her bamboo clapper, nor dived and bathed in the pool; she did not think, and the lie told the truth; hearing it the mother bowed her head, and the girl's going to the field is over, poor thing.
147.nuance: The girl's denial lists, unasked, exactly what the lovers did, so the mother learns everything from it; told in the man's hearing, the comic scene is a warning that the field trysts are ended and only marriage remains.

thinai_evidence.note: millet, parrots and the waterfall hills

148.reading: The friend reassures the woman: he who, looking at her colour and speaking softly, said she could not bear to come there, set out today on his work; they say he is crossing the hard tract along the long waterless stretch where the deep ponds have dried, where in the shade of the red-stemmed kadamba, fearless of the bowmen with their bent bows, a red-eyed tiger, fierce at the kill, springs on the spotted face of a high-tusked bull elephant to end the pangs of his sharp-clawed mate, newly delivered in her rock cave; 'I will not grieve, friend; may his journey prosper.'
148.nuance: The last line can be heard in the woman's own voice, answering the comfort; the colophon gives the whole poem to the friend, who would then be modelling the answer she wants the woman to give.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left for his work across the waste

iraicchi.act: the male tiger hunts the elephant to relieve the hunger of his mate who has just given birth
iraicchi.sense: the man crossing that land is doing the same for the woman he left, so his going is care for her and she may bear it

149.reading: The friend tells the woman that the street women, some and many, glance sidelong and touch forefinger to nose-tip spreading the gossip, and their mother beats her with a little cane; worn out, she has made ready to go with the shore lord whose chariot comes at midnight driven by swift horses whose coloured manes smell of the fresh flowers of the seaside grove they brushed; let this clamouring town carry its gossip and be done.
149.nuance: The friend says 'I have made ready to go' (யானே) for the woman, speaking as one with her. The finger on the nose-tip is the town's gesture of scandal, the cane the house's answer, and the elopement is the answer to both. The colophon files it under neythal by its shore things; its situation is the elopement of paalai.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைவியை உடன்போக்கு வலித்தது சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the decision to leave home with the man

150.reading: The courtesan tells the bard that his lord is a fine joke: like the holders of strong forts who bow and cry 'long live Vazhuthi', whose warring army scattered elephants to break the guard-forest and took many forts, he bowed here, then said he cares nothing at all for it; he drove his prancing horse into her street, showed his garland and chaplet and took her whole heart; will he let it go now? Her mother, cane in hand, is furious and will not relent.
150.nuance: The Pandya's conquests are borrowed as a measure of submission: the lord is mocked as a vassal who paid homage and then denied it.

colophon.thurai: தலைநின்று ஒழுகப்படா நின்ற பரத்தை தலைவனை நெருங்கிப் பாணற்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan's quarrel over the lord, through his bard

comparisons.tenor: the lord who first bowed to her and then disowned her

151.reading: With the man listening, the friend says that even if the girl's fair forehead pales and her broad shoulders grow thin, may the hill lord not come by night, from the slope where a white-tusked elephant, its tusk reddened after goring a fierce tiger at a narrow pass, washes it in the waterfall on the rock, and where a red-faced she-monkey who mated in secret on the pepper-vine slope, afraid that the male's great leaf-eating troop will find out, bends over the deep pool and smooths her tousled hair before climbing the flowering branch of the gold-clustered vengai.
151.nuance: The elephant washing the tiger's blood from its tusk is the danger of the night path, told as scene; the monkey is the lovers' secret.

thinai_evidence.note: monkey, vengai and pepper slopes of the hill country

ullurai.tenor: the girl and the hill lord meeting secretly by night

pairs.situation: the fear that her kin and the town will learn of it
the girl must hide the traces of the meeting before she is seen

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a monkey of the kurinji slopes in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

152.reading: The man set on the palmyra-stem horse says, so the friend will hear, that love gave him the madal and the blossoms of the close-strung erukku gave him gossip; the sun, fond in its work, gave him loneliness as its bright rays dimmed and it crossed the evening sky; and on top of all that, as the north wind gently scatters spray, night too gave him helplessness, mixed with the weary call of the andril joined with its mate in the nest; what will become of him, pitiable as he is.
152.nuance: அலர் is both the blossom of the erukku and the town's gossip: the flower he wears is the talk he earns. Each line gives one hour its own gift of pain. The andril joined with its mate only calls; it does nothing a lover does, so it is scene, not iraicchi.

colophon.thurai: மடல் வலித்த தலைவன்முன்னிலைப் புறமொழியாக தோழி கேட்பச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the madal and its erukku garland, the lover's public ride

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he addresses no one present; he speaks of himself so the friend will hear

153.reading: The woman, wasting in separation, says that as the sweet-voiced cloud that scooped up the eastern sea, rose westward darkening, flashed like a smith's pot pouring copper so that the earth shone, and its work done everywhere went off to the south and was spent, so her heart has gone to him and stayed there; her body, left here, lives on by eating, like the lone man who stayed to guard the ruins of a great town whose people fled when the furious king of mighty wars struck it.
153.nuance: The poet is named Thanimakanaar, the lone man, from line 10. The body is not dead but a caretaker of an emptied place: it eats so that something remains to guard.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman left behind while her heart goes after the absent man

comparisons.tenor: the cloud's lightning
her heart that has gone to him and not come back
her body, left behind and kept alive only by eating

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; she speaks of herself

154.reading: With the man listening, the woman asks her friend whether she can sleep, not hearing it: the forest has fallen silent, the sky spreads a pitch dark as if to split the hills, the many-voiced cloud thunders on without pause, and in the cloud-wrapped thicket a fierce gaping-mouthed tiger that has felled an elephant roars fearfully; her heart, scarred by great distress, would cool like fire quenched with water if he did not come tonight, for each time she thinks of the hard path through the hills that bar the slope, her unrestrained heart runs out over the ground.
154.nuance: She would rather he did not come than come through such a night, which tells the listening man that the night meetings must end in marriage. தூவிலாட்டி in line 7 is a rare form of address.

thinai_evidence.note: tiger, elephant and the hill slopes of the night path

comparisons.tenor: the pitch darkness spread over the sky
her scarred heart that would cool if he stayed away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; by the poem it is the woman (என் நிறை இல் நெஞ்சே)

155.reading: The man tells how, meeting her a second time, he said to her: you do not play the orai game with your bright-jewelled companions, you do not wear a garland of broad-petalled neythal, you stand apart in the flowering seaside grove; who are you? we bow to you and ask: with a beauty no one tires of seeing, are you a goddess who lives in the wide sea of clear waves, or have you settled on the bank of the dark backwater? speak now, girl; and in answer her sharp-toothed smile opened, and tears spread over her many-petalled kohl eyes.
155.nuance: She answers his question only with a smile and tears, which no goddess would give: the reply settles that she is a woman. The colophon files it under neythal by its shore; the situation, a meeting of lovers, is the punarthal of kurinji.

colophon.thurai: இரண்டாம் கூட்டத்துத்தலைவியை எதிர்ப்பட்டுத் தலைவன் சொல்லியது உணர்ப்பு வயின் வாரா ஊடற்கண் தலைவன் சொற்றதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the man's approach at a meeting of the lovers before marriage

comparisons.tenor: the girl, too beautiful to be human

occasion.words: உணர்ப்பு வயின் வாரா ஊடற்கண் தலைவன் சொற்றதூஉம் ஆம்

156.reading: The friend tells the lord of the great rocky hills that his coming through darkness where feet cannot find the way, slipping past the guard of their wide house, shows his great love; but they, singing of him and his hill, will guard the small millet for many days and will go there, so let him come by day and end their many cares; for the people of their hamlet on the great hill of tall reeds, though they have drunk their toddy, are formidable, and the swaying rain has settled on their high-peaked hill, roaring in the rock clefts.
156.nuance: She refuses the night only by offering the day: the millet field the girls guard is the place she names for the meeting.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field and the hill hamlet

157.reading: Away for wealth, the man tells his heart, which has sensed the season, that now, after the great rains that served the world's labour, in early summer when the river sand is rippled fine like the back of a spotted moving snake, each time the paired koel calls from the cluster-laden mango, the dark girl with fine scattered freckles, like the pollen shed by the tall vengai beside the low rocks of the forest, will think of them and weep greatly as she hears it.
157.nuance: The paired koel only calls: its sound carries the season's pain but it does nothing a lover does, so it is scene, not iraicchi. He measures her grief by his own heart, which has already felt the season.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரிந்த தலைவன் பருவம் உணர்ந்த நெஞ்சிற்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the man away from her imagines her weeping at the season

comparisons.tenor: the river sand rippled by the shrinking stream
her fine freckles

158.reading: With the man listening, the woman tells her friend that she has not seen it, for it lies hidden, the path the lord of the high hills comes by: there the stony track must surely break the feet, the thick darkness must surely put out the eyes, and a fierce tiger from a cleft in the rocks, having struck a spotted-faced elephant till it cries out, wipes its fat-cheeked, blood-drinking mouth against the trunk of a vengai.
158.nuance: Her fear is all imagination: she has never seen the path (யானோ காணேன்), and the tiger wiping its mouth on the vengai is what her mind sets on it.

colophon.thurai: ஆறு பார்த்து உற்ற அச்சத்தால் சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: tiger, elephant and vengai of the hill path

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

occasion.words: ஆறு பார்த்து உற்ற அச்சத்தால் சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; by the poem it is the woman

159.reading: The friend tells the man that on the great flower-strewn shore heaped up by the strong waves of the dark wide sea, gleaming like cut sapphire, on the steep sand dune piled like moonlight, they pass the day counting the lines of herons like clustered conches; then if they say 'rise, let us go to the rich house with its punnai yard swept and patterned by the wind, where fat fish are eaten', she will not agree, and they cannot tell her 'stay'; so let the chariot he loves lodge tonight in the little fishing hamlet that sleeps to the sound of breaking waves, so that it wakes in uproar.
159.nuance: The request that his chariot stay the night is a demand for publicity: a hamlet woken by it will know, and what the town knows must end in marriage.

colophon.thurai: தலைவியின் ஆற்றாமையும் உலகியலும் கூறி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: herons, punnai and fish of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the dark wide sea
the white sand dune
the line of herons

160.reading: The man answers his friend's rebuke: good sense, friendship, shame, decency, usefulness, character and conduct that knows what is fitting, he once knew them better than his friend does, before he saw the wide, cool, intoxicating eyes of this girl, like a garland of facing kuvalai blossoms bloomed in an old pond, with her young breasts flecked with freckles, the fine pale spots as if sprinkled, her hair dressed in five parts and her fragrant locks over a fair forehead marked with a red dot.
160.nuance: He does not deny the virtues his friend preaches; he claims to know them better, so the rebuke teaches him nothing. The list of virtues runs two lines; the list of her features runs seven.

thinai_evidence.note: a man struck by a girl at first sight, before any union

comparisons.vehicle: முது நீர் இலஞ்சிப் பூத்த குவளை எதிர் மலர்ப் பிணையல்
comparisons.tenor: her eyes
the fine pale spots on her breasts

links.note: Both compare a woman's hair to the bright ripples (அறல்) of a named river: the Arisil by Killi's Ambar in Natrinai 141, the forest stream north of Vaanan's Sirukudi in Akananuru 117.
links.teaches: The one simile marks the two ends of the girl's story: in Natrinai 141 the river-dark hair is what keeps the lover from leaving her, and in Akananuru 117 it is the mother's last picture of the daughter who left with him, dressed now by his hands.

links.note: Kural 84: the goddess of fortune dwells gladly in the house of one who tends good guests with a glad face. Natrinai 142 sets the wife who rejoices at a guest even at night in a woodland of unfailing plenty (பொய்யா யாணர்).
links.teaches: The poem gives the couplet's householder a face and a hour: the glad host is the waiting wife, her welcome extends even to guests who arrive after dark, and the plenty the Kural promises is already the landscape the returning husband drives through.

links.note: Akananuru 165: onlookers see the mother after the elopement rest under the nochchi the girl touched and embrace her doll. Natrinai 143: the mother herself weeps at the playmates and the nochchi and confesses she noticed the scent of the girl's hair and said nothing.
links.teaches: Held together, the two give the mother's grief from outside and from inside: what onlookers see as pure loss, her own words show to include guilt, since she read the signs in the girl's hair, heard the gossip, and chose silence.

links.note: In Akananuru 117 the foster mother asks whether the hair she once combed and the girl would not let her wash now falls loose, dressed with her lover's flowers; in Natrinai 143 the mother recalls telling the girl her hair smelled fragrant.
links.teaches: Both mothers read the daughter's love in her hair, one before the flight and one after: the fragrance the mother let pass in Natrinai 143 is the lover's flowers that Akananuru 117 imagines on the road, so the hair is the household's evidence of a bond it could see but not stop.

links.note: Kuruntokai 17: when love hardens, men ride the palm stem as a horse, wear erukku buds as flowers and are jeered in the street. Natrinai 146 addresses such a rider in his erukku chaplet and promises that kind people will gather and offer him shade like a just king's umbrella.
links.teaches: The street that mocks the madal rider in Kuruntokai 17 is also the street that pities him in Natrinai 146; set side by side they show that the ride works by public feeling, ridicule and compassion together, which is what presses the girl's people to yield.

links.note: In Akananuru 28 the friend warns that if the girl will not scare the parrots her mother will send others to guard the millet and the lover will be out of reach. In Natrinai 147 the parrots have taken the millet, the mother questions her, her denial gives her away, and her going to the field is over.
links.teaches: The two friends' speeches are the before and after of one plot: the warning of Akananuru 28 comes true in Natrinai 147, and the second poem shows how, through the girl's own guilty denial rather than through the parrots.

links.note: Kural 1151: if you are not going, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Natrinai 148 ends, after the man has gone for his work, with 'I will not grieve, friend; may his journey prosper'.
links.teaches: On the same departure for work the two voices take incompatible stands, the couplet refusing all comfort as if the going were a death, the poem blessing the journey; the iraicchi of the tiger hunting for its mate shows how the friend's comfort turns the one stance into the other.

links.note: Kural 1147: the town's gossip is the manure and the mother's words the water of this sickness. In Natrinai 149 the street women spread the gossip, the mother beats the girl with a cane, and she resolves to leave with the shore lord.
links.teaches: The couplet says that gossip and the mother's scolding feed the love they mean to kill; the poem shows what that fed love finally does, turning the same two pressures, the street's finger at the nose and the mother's cane, into the reason for elopement.

links.note: Kuruntokai 32: if one can tell morning, day, helpless evening, midnight and dawn apart, love is false. Natrinai 152's lover tells the hours exactly: the sun as it dims gave him loneliness, and the night with the andril's call gave him helplessness.
links.teaches: On one reading the claims are incompatible: Kuruntokai 32 makes losing track of the hours the proof of true love, while Natrinai 152 gives a lover whose love is real precisely because each hour is known by its own fresh pain, so knowing the clock is no sign of coolness.

links.note: Kural 1133: he once had shame and manliness, and now has the palmyra horse that lovers ride. Natrinai 152: love gave him the madal, the erukku gave him gossip, the sun gave loneliness, night gave helplessness.
links.teaches: The couplet records one exchange, virtues lost for a madal; the poem turns it into a chain of gifts in which each thing hands on the next harm, so the madal is not the end of the loss but the first link of a day-long sequence.

links.note: Kural 338: the bond of body and life is like a bird that flies off leaving its nest alone. Natrinai 153: her heart has gone after him and her body, left behind, lives on by eating, like the lone man guarding a ruined town.
links.teaches: The poem shows the couplet's departure without the death: the heart flies off as the life does in the Kural, yet the body stays, sustained only to keep watch over its own emptiness, so separation in love is a death the body is made to outlive.

links.note: Kural 1081: on first seeing her the man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman. Natrinai 155: at their second meeting he asks her aloud whether she is the goddess of the sea or of the backwater, and she answers with a smile and tears.
links.teaches: The couplet leaves the man's doubt as a question in his head; the poem puts the same question to the girl and lets her answer it, since a smile and tears are a woman's reply, not a goddess's, so the doubt is settled by her response.

links.note: In Akananuru 118 the friend fears gossip if the hero comes by day and fears the tiger still more if he comes alone at midnight, and says the girl has stopped the millet songs. In Natrinai 156 the friend refuses the night tryst and asks him to come by day, since they will guard the millet for many days.
links.teaches: The two friends weigh the same choice of day or night and decide it by the millet: while the girls still guard the field, as in Natrinai 156, the day offers a safe meeting place, and once the guarding has stopped, as in Akananuru 118, day and night are both closed and only marriage is left.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 14 the man wishes that once he wins the girl the town would know it and many in the street would call him the good woman's husband. In Natrinai 159 the friend asks him to let his chariot lodge in the fishing hamlet so that it wakes in uproar.
links.teaches: Both treat the town's knowing as the way to marriage, but from opposite sides: the man in Kuruntokai 14 wishes for it after winning her, while the friend in Natrinai 159 demands it now as the means of winning her, using the hamlet's noise as pressure.

links.note: Kuruntokai 58: the man tells his rebuking friends it would be well if they could hold back his sickness, but it has spread like butter melting on a hot rock. Natrinai 160: he tells his rebuker that he knew good sense, shame and conduct better than him, before he saw her eyes.
links.teaches: These are two answers to the same rebuke: one grants that the friends' aim is good and says no one can carry it out, the other says the friend's lesson is one he already knew best, so together they show the rebuke fails not for lack of knowledge but because sight of her has overridden it.

links.note: Kural 1133: he once had shame and manliness, and now has the madal. Natrinai 160: shame, decency and good conduct he knew better than his friend, before he saw her.
links.teaches: The couplet says the virtues were possessed and are now gone; the poem says they are still known, better than the rebuker knows them, and simply no longer govern him, so love takes away their rule, not the knowledge of them.

source_issues: 142 line 3 is a repaired line (lost vowel sign ொ restored, flagged by show); marked as repaired.
150 line 5: '·' is the old encoding of ஃ (flagged); marked as அஃது. Lines 2-6 (the Vazhuthi simile and who says 'we care nothing for it') are hard to construe; the verse is marked uncertain.
153 line 1 recurs word for word as Natrinai 346 line 1 (flagged); marked as written.
160: the record names no poet, and line 1 is not in sangamtamil.com (flagged); marked as our text has it.

143, 154 and 158: the colophon thurai names no speaker; the speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem. 144's thurai reads ஆற்றது ஏதத்திற்குக்கவன்று, apparently for ஆற்றினது ஏதத்திற்குக் கவன்று; copied as written.
146 lines 6-11: the construction (who gathers, who is 'skilled in saying we are good', what the heart does) is uncertain; marked uncertain. 154 line 7 தூவிலாட்டி is a rare form; marked uncertain.
Thinai differs from the colophon in 146 and 152 (madal, perunthinai by porul), 149 (elopement, paalai by uri) and 155 (lovers' meeting, kurinji by uri); the colophon is copied unchanged.
